newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwait papers welcome Stealths, U.S. support.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait papers welcome Stealths, U.S. support.

text.p: Kuwaiti newspapers on Saturday welcomed a U.S. military buildup in the Gulf, saying it sent a firm message that Washington would defend oil-rich allies during heightened tension between Baghdad and its Gulf War foes.

The government has not yet responded to Iraq's announcement that it was suspending missile attacks on U.S. and allied warplanes enforcing no-fly zones over Iraq, a step Baghdad said it hoped would help defuse the crisis with the United States.

Commentators and editorial writers said most Kuwaitis were reassured by the arrival on Friday evening of U.S. F-117A Stealth bombers despite Iraqi warnings that their mission in Kuwait was tantamount to an act of war by the small Gulf state.

"Hosting these planes and their crews is not an easy burden for Kuwait, but Kuwaitis are willing to offer a lot to those who stood by them during their crisis," columnist and former oil official Sheikh Ali Jaber al-Ali al-Sabah wrote in al-Seyassah.
"What did Iraq expect us to do in reply to its silly threats? Did they expect us to sit back and allow them to invade us the way they did before?" columnist Fouad al-Hashem wrote in al-Watan daily.

Eight of the radar-evading Stealth planes flew into Kuwait's Ahmad al-Jaber air base on a mission U.S. officials said could involve punishing Iraq for firing at American planes patrolling an Iraqi southern no-fly zone on Wednesday.

Sheikh Ali added: "As to the security concerns of the crews of these aircraft, we confirm as Kuwaitis that they are our sons. They can sleep in our houses for protection if need be, and if any lunatic in Kuwait tries to offend or attack them he will be severely punished by civilians and the security system of Kuwait."

Newspapers said Crown Prince and Prime Minister Sheikh Saad al-Abdulla al-Sabah was expected to make a rare visit to parliament on Saturday for an emergency debate on the tensions with Baghdad, the latest in a series of flare-ups between the two countries since Iraq invaded and occupied Kuwait in 1990-91.

Kuwaitis said Sheikh Saad was expected to reply to the Iraqi announcement on Friday evening that Baghdad would not challenge the no-fly zone, which Washington expanded last week to punish Baghdad for attacks on northern Iraqi Kurds.

The withdrawal of Iraq's vow to shoot at planes flying over its territory followed orders last week by Saddam to his air defence gunners and pilots to down American, British and French aircraft policing the zones.
Ahmad al-Jarallah, editor-in-chief of Seyassah and its sister paper the English-language Arab Times, wrote that Kuwaitis still wanted to see Saddam toppled.
"We hope the world would strike directly at Saddam's head, to rectify a mistake of 1991, when coalition forces stopped short (of toppling Saddam) after the liberation of Kuwait," he wrote.
A dissenting view came from anti-American political scientist Abdullah al-Nafisi, who wrote: "What does the United States want from this uncalled-for confrontation with Iraq?

"American policy since 1991 until now has been a cause of increased tension in the Gulf," he wrote, complaining that U.S. policy involved "blackmail to support its assets and its political and economic capacities".
"It is in the best interests of the Americans to review their unbalanced policies."
